Notes on a Day Spent Wandering

I woke up this morning before the alarm, which is something that almost never happens, and lay there for a while listening to the house settle into itself. The radiator ticked once, as if clearing its throat, and somewhere downstairs the fridge hummed its low, indifferent note, and through the thin curtains I could see that the light had that pale, washed-out quality which promises either a very fine day or a day that will rain in the most sideways and uncommitted way possible. I did not reach for my phone. It was an effort, a small, deliberate act of disobedience, and I noticed how my hand twitched toward the bedside table even as my mind told it not to. Instead I made tea, stood by the kitchen window with the mug warming my palms, and watched a neighbor unlock his bicycle and wheel it, thoughtfully, to the end of his drive, where he seemed to reconsider the entire enterprise and wheel it back again. There was no urgency in anything, and for the first time in weeks that felt like a gift rather than a failure.

The strange guilt of unscheduled time is something I have only lately learned to name. As an adult, most of my hours arrive pre-claimed, assigned a purpose and a metric, and even my leisure is usually optimized, measured in steps or finished pages or episodes watched, as if rest itself had to justify its existence by producing some evidence of improvement. To have a day with no appointment in it feels faintly scandalous, like skipping a meeting with myself. I kept catching an impulse to invent a task, to clean the skirting boards or reorganize the pantry or finally answer those emails that have been sitting in my inbox like unopened letters from a more responsible version of me. But I decided, perhaps out of laziness and perhaps out of a dawning curiosity, to let the day remain unclaimed, to see what would happen if I simply walked out of the front door and followed whatever caught my eye. It was not a grand experiment. It was merely a willingness to be led by small things.

Maps are a wonderful and terrible invention. They give you the illusion that a place is known once its outline is familiar, that to have traced a route a dozen times is to have understood it. I have walked these streets for years, more or less, and I can get from the bakery to the bus stop to the library without looking up, following the grooves worn into my habits. But this morning I left the map in my head at home. I turned down a lane I have always meant to explore but never have, a narrow passage between two houses where the pavement dips and the bins are always out and a cat, a fat marmalade cat, sits with great seriousness on a wall. I had always assumed it was a dead end, a service alley with nothing at the end of it but more bins. Today I discovered it opens, after a squeeze past a leaning fence, onto a small courtyard where someone grows tomatoes in a row of identical tin cans, and where the washing lines of three houses cross in a bright, tangled geometry overhead. It was not beautiful, exactly, but it was alive in a way my familiar route was not.

Childhood wandering was different because the world was sized for it. Then, a street could go on forever, and an afternoon could be an entire civilization of forts and expeditions and grievous injuries sustained in the line of duty. I remember the deep seriousness with which we planned those expeditions, the hand-drawn maps with X marking places that were, in reality, a shrub and a discarded sofa, the solemn oaths not to return home until signals were sent or supplies ran out. We were not killing time; we were inhabiting it completely, the way you inhabit a house you have just moved into and are still learning the creaks of. Somewhere along the way, walking became transportation rather than exploration, a means of getting from one point to another with maximum efficiency and minimum deviation, and the world narrowed to corridors. I think I missed the feeling of a place being larger than my errands, and perhaps that is why I was excited, in a quiet and slightly embarrassed way, by the prospect of being a flâneur in my own neighborhood.

The town I live in is a coastal town, which is a particular kind of place with its own weather and its own temperament. The sea is always present even when you cannot see it, in the salt that stiffens a coat, in the cries of gulls that sound perpetually outraged about something, in the way the light changes at four in the afternoon as if someone had turned a dial. The town has the usual mixture of pride and neglect that comes from being somewhere people pass through on their way to somewhere more famous. There are grand Victorian houses with peeling paint and elegant proportions, and there are buildings from the sixties that look like they were designed by someone who had only heard of architecture described to them secondhand. The harbor is mostly pleasure boats now, bobbing and nudging each other in the swell, and the old fish market is a café with a chalkboard that misspells scones. None of it is pristine, and that is precisely its charm; it has the look of a place that has been loved intermittently, by different generations, in different ways.

I walked down to the harbor first, because the sea has a way of rearranging your thoughts. The tide was out, leaving a wide expanse of wet sand and stranded rock pools that glittered like something dropped and forgotten. An old man in waders was hunting for something with a bucket and a fork, moving slowly and with great concentration, as if the shore were a library and he were looking for a particular book. A woman was walking two dogs of wildly different sizes, one of them trotting with enormous dignity and the other apparently convinced that every lamp post contained a secret worth investigating. The wind came off the water in sudden, companionable gusts, lifting the corners of my coat and carrying with it the smell of salt and diesel and, faintly, chips. I stood for a while and did nothing in particular, which is to say I watched the boats strain at their moorings and the gulls perform their aerial disputes, and I tried to remember the last time I had stood somewhere simply to be in it, rather than to pass through it on the way to a better view.

The baker was halfway through his first batch when I arrived, and the warm, yeasty air spilled out onto the pavement each time the door opened. Inside, the counter was a small museum of brownness, rolls and loaves and buns in every shade from pale gold to near-black, arranged with a care that suggested both pride and an understanding that people do choose with their eyes first. I bought a roll and a coffee, though I did not need either, and took them to sit on the low wall outside, where a sparrow hopped around my feet with an optimism that bordered on delusion. The baker came out with a tray of something hot and dusted it with flour, and we exchanged the kind of brief, weather-based conversation that is the small change of community. He told me the ovens had been temperamental all week, that the sea air got into everything, that his father had baked in this same shop and had claimed the rolls rose better when it rained. I told him I hoped that was true, because the forecast looked promising, and he laughed and said the weather was the only thing in town that kept its promises, and even then only by accident.

Small conversations are a kind of currency that has been devalued by our reluctance to spend it. We have become so practiced at moving through public space with our attention elsewhere, earbuds in, eyes forward, that a stranger speaking to us feels like an interruption rather than an invitation. But today I found myself in several of them, and each one altered the texture of the day in a way I had not anticipated. A woman in the bookshop asked what I was reading, and when I said I was not, strictly speaking, reading anything at the moment, she took this as a challenge and recommended three books with the enthusiasm of a missionary. In the post office, a man behind me in the queue asked if I knew whether the parcel service had improved, and we spent five minutes elaborating a shared theory that nothing had improved since approximately 1987. None of these exchanges were significant. All of them were human in a way that left me feeling less like a solitary figure moving through a painted backdrop and more like a resident of an actual place, temporarily borrowed by an actual community.

The bookshop is not, technically, a bookshop anymore. It is a secondhand bookshop and a record shop and a place where someone sells handmade soap and a place where, on Saturdays, a man tunes pianos in the back room. It has the wonderful, musty smell of paper and dust and old wood, and the shelves lean at angles that suggest decades of gentle surrender. I went in with no intention of buying anything and emerged, as always, with a biography of a lighthouse keeper, a poetry collection with a cracked spine, and a novel I had already read twice but which I somehow felt needed rescuing from the classics table. The joy of such a place is its total indifference to algorithm and relevance. No one has optimized the stock for my demographic. The books are there because someone, at some point, decided to keep them, and the order is mostly alphabetical except where it is mostly by size, and except where it is neither. I spent an hour pulling volumes out at random and reading the first paragraph, that small, arbitrary act of judgment which has led me astray more reliably than any other in my life. There was a book about weather, which seemed appropriate, and a book about the history of walking, which seemed like a taunt, and a children's book about a bear who wanted to be a lighthouse. I bought the one about weather.

Boredom, I am coming to believe, is a vastly underrated state of mind. We treat it as a problem to be solved instantly with a screen, a podcast, a quick scroll through the evidence that other people are having more interesting lives and different kinds of cake. But boredom has a useful function; it is the mind's way of clearing its throat and asking what, exactly, it is doing here. When I am bored, my thoughts slow down and begin to wander in ways they do not when I am occupied, and they make connections that feel less like productivity and more like discovery. Today, sitting on a bench because my feet had decided they had done enough for the moment, I found my mind drifting from the price of cheese to the design of benches to the fact that I had never once, in all my years here, actually sat on this particular bench, though I had passed it a thousand times. I watched the clouds arrange themselves into temporary continents and watched a cyclist struggle with a child seat and watched, with great interest, the progress of a small ladybird making its way across the armrest. It was not a wasted half hour. It was, I think, the most productive thing I did all day, though nothing I could list on a form would capture it.

By late morning the rain had arrived, as forecast and as promised. It did not come in a dramatic downpour but in a fine, persistent mist that softened all the edges and turned the streets into shining versions of themselves. I took shelter under the awning of a closed shop, where a poster advertising a lost cat had been curling in the damp for what looked like a year, and where a small group of us, strangers to one another, performed the elaborate choreography of people pretending not to be waiting for the same thing. A woman with a shopping trolley and a very determined umbrella, a schoolboy with a plastic bag held over his hair, an elderly man walking a dachshund in a knitted coat. The rain made us temporary conspirators. The schoolboy asked the elderly man if his dog was cold, and the elderly man said the dog was always cold, that it was a breed preference, and that in any case the coat was his wife's idea and the dog had strong feelings about it. We all laughed at this, and the rain seemed, briefly, like a shared joke rather than an inconvenience. When it eased, we went our separate ways with an odd sense of having been in something together.

I had lunch in a small café that seats six people and serves soup that changes depending on the mood of the person making it. Today it was lentil, thick enough to stand a spoon in, with bread that had been toasted and then, perhaps as an afterthought, buttered. I sat by the window and watched the wet street and read the first chapter of my rescued novel, and I was gratified by the way a good book can make a small room feel larger, as if the walls had been politely asked to move back a little. The owner, who knows my face but not, as far as I can tell, my name, brought over an extra roll without being asked and said it was going stale, which was clearly a lie of the most benevolent kind. I ate slowly. There is a particular pleasure in eating a meal without a screen, without a schedule, without the sense that the fork is competing with a clock. The soup was hot and the rain had stopped and for a moment the whole world narrowed to the steam rising from the bowl and the comfortable weight of a book in my pocket, and I felt, in a way I rarely do, entirely present in my own life.

In the afternoon I went to the post office to post a letter I had written two days ago and which had been sitting on the mantelpiece developing a sense of entitlement. It was a real letter, on paper, in an envelope, with a stamp that cost more than I remembered stamps costing, which led to a brief and silent reckoning with time. The letter was to a friend who lives in another country and who communicates, as I do, mostly in the brief, apologetic messages that accumulate in the spaces between our actual lives. Writing it had taken me an evening, and I had crossed out whole sentences and started again, trying to find a tone that was neither too formal nor too casual, which is, I suspect, the entire difficulty of saying anything true to anyone. Posting it felt like releasing something into a slower system, one that would take days to move across continents and that would arrive, eventually, in a physical form that could be held and put on a fridge and returned to. I was absurdly pleased with myself, in the way one is pleased with a child who has learned to tie a shoe: a small competence, long delayed, finally accomplished.

After that I climbed the hill, because a walk that does not include a hill feels incomplete, like a story without a middle. The path goes up between allotments where people grow things with more enthusiasm than skill, and past a graveyard where the oldest stones lean at dramas angles, and then it emerges onto the common, a wide, windy expanse of grass that belongs to everyone and to no one. From the top you can see the whole town arranged like a model of itself: the harbor, the Victorian houses, the sixties blocks, the church spire puncturing the sky like a punctuation mark. The view has the curious effect of making my concerns smaller without making them less real. The emails and the deadlines and the vague sense of falling behind were still there, somewhere below, but from this height they looked like what they were, which is to say temporary arrangements made by a person who had, for the moment, decided to arrange things differently. The wind was strong and the grass bent in waves, and I stood there with my hands in my pockets feeling, briefly and completely, like a figure in a landscape painting, which is not a bad way to feel on a Tuesday.

Children were playing on the common, in that loose, unorganized way that seems to have survived despite all our best efforts to schedule it out of existence. They had invented a game involving a stick, a ball, and a set of rules that changed every three minutes in response to injustice. There was a dispute about whether the stick was magic or merely a stick, and a solemn negotiation about boundaries, and a moment of high drama when the ball rolled into a bush and was declared, by unanimous vote, to have been stolen by a dragon. I watched them for a while from a distance, not because I am particularly nostalgic for childhood, which I remember as being mostly a series of minor humiliations and excellent snacks, but because there is something clarifying about watching people who have not yet learned to apologize for taking up space. They were loud and inefficient and utterly absorbed, and the game was entirely pointless, and that was precisely why it mattered. I thought about how many of my own activities are designed to be useful, and how few of them produce the kind of joy that comes from making something up and then believing in it completely for an afternoon.

I stopped at the lighthouse on my way back down, though it is not a working lighthouse anymore and has been a museum and a café and, for a brief period in the eighties, a disco, according to a plaque that seemed to be trying not to dwell on the matter. The museum itself was closed, but the tower was open, and I climbed the winding stairs in the company of a school group who were asking the kind of questions that suggest a diet of quiz shows. How high is it? Can you see France? What happens if you drop a penny? The answers, delivered by a volunteer with the patience of a saint, had the satisfying solidity of facts that have been repeated many times to many generations of curious children. At the top, the wind was even stronger, and the glass was thick and scratched by a century of visitors pressing their faces to it. The sea stretched out in all directions, indifferent and magnificent, and the town below looked like a collection of toys that someone had arranged with love and then forgotten to put away. I stayed longer than was reasonable, just looking, and the volunteer, who had seen this before, said nothing at all, which was exactly right.

There is a temptation, when describing a day like this, to make it sound like a revelation, as if I had returned home a different person, enlightened and serene and ready to throw away my phone and take up weaving. The truth is more modest and, I think, more useful. I came home with wet shoes, a biography of a lighthouse keeper I will probably not finish, and a faint sense of having noticed things. I made tea again, stood at the same window, and watched the light go out of the day in the slow, gradual way that evening light does when nobody is rushing it. The neighbor was unlocking his bicycle again, or perhaps it was a different neighbor, or perhaps it was the same one on a different errand, and I waved, and he waved back, and we neither of us went anywhere in particular. The house settled around me with its familiar creaks and hums. My mind, unaccustomed to idleness, drifted through the day's inventory: the cat on the wall, the sparrow by the bakery, the ladybird on the bench, the dachshund in its coat, the dragon in the bush. It was not a list of achievements. It was a list of witnesses.

Wandering, I have come to think, is not the opposite of purpose. It is a different kind of purpose, one that cannot be measured in outcomes but can be measured in attention. To walk without a destination is to give the world a chance to speak first, to let it offer up its tomatoes in tin cans and its soup of uncertain provenance and its letters that take a week to arrive. It is a small act of trust, the belief that if you are patient and unhurried and slightly curious, something interesting will happen, even if that something is only a fat cat sitting with great seriousness on a wall. In a culture that treats every minute as a resource to be mined, wandering is a form of resistance, not loud or dramatic, but persistent and quietly joyful. It says that a day can be valuable even if nothing was accomplished, that time spent noticing is not time wasted, that the map is not the territory and that sometimes the best route is the one you did not plan to take.

So tomorrow, or perhaps the day after tomorrow, if the rain holds off and the radiator behaves itself, I will do it again. I will leave the phone on the table and walk out without a destination, and I will turn down the lane I have always meant to explore. I will buy a roll I do not need and accept the extra one I did not ask for. I will sit on a bench I have passed a thousand times and watch the ladybird, or its descendant, make its slow progress. I will not be transformed. I will not be suddenly wise. But I will be, for a few hours, exactly where I am, in a particular place, on a particular day, paying attention to the small, unremarkable, entirely sufficient business of being alive in the world. And that, I suspect, is more than enough to be going on with.

The wind was strong and the grass bent in waves, and I stood there with my hands in my pockets feeling, briefly and completely, like a figure in a landscape painting, which is not a bad way to feel on a Tuesday.

Children were playing on the common, in that loose, unorganized way that seems to have survived despite all our best efforts to schedule it out of existence. They had invented a game involving a stick, a ball, and a set of rules that changed every three minutes in response to injustice. There was a dispute about whether the stick was magic or merely a stick, and a solemn negotiation about boundaries, and a moment of high drama when the ball rolled into a bush and was declared, by unanimous vote, to have been stolen by a dragon. I watched them for a while from a distance, not because I am particularly nostalgic for childhood, which I remember as being mostly a series of minor humiliations and excellent snacks, but because there is something clarifying about watching people who have not yet learned to apologize for taking up space. They were loud and inefficient and utterly absorbed, and the game was entirely pointless, and that was precisely why it mattered. I thought about how many of my own activities are designed to be useful, and how few of them produce the kind of joy that comes from making something up and then believing in it completely for an afternoon.

I stopped at the lighthouse on my way back down, though it is not a working lighthouse anymore and has been a museum and a café and, for a brief period in the eighties, a disco, according to a plaque that seemed to be trying not to dwell on the matter. The museum itself was closed, but the tower was open, and I climbed the winding stairs in the company of a school group who were asking the kind of questions that suggest a diet of quiz shows. How high is it? Can you see France? What happens if you drop a penny? The answers, delivered by a volunteer with the patience of a saint, had the satisfying solidity of facts that have been repeated many times to many generations of curious children. At the top, the wind was even stronger, and the glass was thick and scratched by a century of visitors pressing their faces to it. The sea stretched out in all directions, indifferent and magnificent, and the town below looked like a collection of toys that someone had arranged with love and then forgotten to put away. I stayed longer than was reasonable, just looking, and the volunteer, who had seen this before, said nothing at all, which was exactly right.

There is a temptation, when describing a day like this, to make it sound like a revelation, as if I had returned home a different person, enlightened and serene and ready to throw away my phone and take up weaving. The truth is more modest and, I think, more useful. I came home with wet shoes, a biography of a lighthouse keeper I will probably not finish, and a faint sense of having noticed things. I made tea again, stood at the same window, and watched the light go out of the day in the slow, gradual way that evening light does when nobody is rushing it. The neighbor was unlocking his bicycle again, or perhaps it was a different neighbor, or perhaps it was the same one on a different errand, and I waved, and he waved back, and we neither of us went anywhere in particular. The house settled around me with its familiar creaks and hums. My mind, unaccustomed to idleness, drifted through the day's inventory: the cat on the wall, the sparrow by the bakery, the ladybird on the bench, the dachshund in its coat, the dragon in the bush. It was not a list of achievements. It was a list of witnesses.

Wandering, I have come to think, is not the opposite of purpose. It is a different kind of purpose, one that cannot be measured in outcomes but can be measured in attention. To walk without a destination is to give the world a chance to speak first, to let it offer up its tomatoes in tin cans and its soup of uncertain provenance and its letters that take a week to arrive. It is a small act of trust, the belief that if you are patient and unhurried and slightly curious, something interesting will happen, even if that something is only a fat cat sitting with great seriousness on a wall. In a culture that treats every minute as a resource to be mined, wandering is a form of resistance, not loud or dramatic, but persistent and quietly joyful. It says that a day can be valuable even if nothing was accomplished, that time spent noticing is not time wasted, that the map is not the territory and that sometimes the best route is the one you did not plan to take.

So tomorrow, or perhaps the day after tomorrow, if the rain holds off and the radiator behaves itself, I will do it again. I will leave the phone on the table and walk out without a destination, and I will turn down the lane I have always meant to explore. I will buy a roll I do not need and accept the extra one I did not ask for. I will sit on a bench I have passed a thousand times and watch the ladybird, or its descendant, make its slow progress. I will not be transformed. I will not be suddenly wise. But I will be, for a few hours, exactly where I am, in a particular place, on a particular day, paying attention to the small, unremarkable, entirely sufficient business of being alive in the world. And that, I suspect, is more than enough to be going on with.
